questions.enonce_markdown:
Comment on the testimonies about Jesus Christ at the beginning of his ministry (John 1;19-51) and show how these testimonies introduce his Christological titles.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** After the prologue (John 1:1-18), which presents Jesus as the Word, the Gospel gives a series of testimonies at the start of his ministry (1:19-51). Different people bear witness to him, and in doing so they give him titles which indicate who he is. This opening function is typical of John: the reader is introduced to the main titles that the rest of the Gospel will develop.

**1. The testimonies and titles.**
- *John the Baptist (1:19-34).* Questioned by priests and Levites, he denies being the Christ, Elijah or the prophet, and says that he is "the voice of one crying in the wilderness" (1:23). He bears witness that Jesus is "the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (1:29, 36), that the Spirit descended and remained on him, and that he is "the Son of God" (1:34). Titles: *Lamb of God*, *Son of God*, one who baptises with the Holy Spirit.
- *Andrew (1:35-42).* After following Jesus he tells his brother Simon "We have found the Messiah" (which is translated Christ). Title: *Messiah/Christ*. Jesus also gives Simon the name Cephas (Peter). The disciples call him *Rabbi*.
- *Philip (1:43-46).* He describes Jesus as the one of whom Moses in the law and the prophets wrote, "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph". Title: the one foretold in the Law and the Prophets.
- *Nathanael (1:47-49).* After Jesus shows knowledge of him, Nathanael confesses: "Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!". Titles: *Son of God*, *King of Israel*.
- *Jesus himself (1:50-51).* He promises greater things and speaks of the angels of God ascending and descending upon the *Son of Man*, recalling Jacob's dream at Bethel (Genesis 28), so that he himself becomes the meeting point between heaven and earth.

**2. How the testimonies introduce Christological titles.**
- Each title looks forward to a later theme: Lamb of God (the Passion, 19:36), Messiah and King (the trial, 18:33-19:22), Son of God (the "Father and Son" theme and the aim of the Gospel, 20:31), Son of Man (the lifting up and glorification, 3:13-14; 12:23).
- The titles come from Jewish expectation (Messiah, King of Israel, the prophet) and from scriptural imagery (Lamb, Son of Man), which shows that Jesus fulfils the hopes of Israel while going beyond them.
- The sequence moves from partial to fuller insight. The disciples begin with "Rabbi", "Messiah" and "King of Israel", but the Son of Man saying promises deeper revelation.
- The theme of witness, introduced here, runs through the whole Gospel (5:31-40), and calls the reader to believe.

**3. Comment.** The testimonies also describe the response of discipleship: "come and see" (1:39, 46), "we have found" and bringing others to Jesus. The titles are given by humans but their full meaning is revealed only by Jesus himself in the rest of the Gospel.

**Conclusion.** John 1:19-51 gives the reader a first and rich portrait of Jesus through human witnesses. The testimonies lay the foundation for the Gospel's Christology and show that the identity of Jesus calls for a response of faith and witness.
